verses.1: Al-Mizan reads the oath as sworn by horses galloping and snorting: ʿadw is rapid running and ḍabḥ the sound of horses’ racing breath. It records readings about pilgrims’ camels from Muzdalifah to Miná and war-camels, but rejects them because the following descriptions do not suit camels.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes fal-mūriyāt qadḥan as horses’ hooves striking stones and pebbly ground so that sparks fly: īrāʾ is kindling and qadḥ striking. It rejects proposed readings of war plots, the kindling of war, or tongues inflaming hostility as weak in this context.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines ighārah as a surprise cavalry attack; it is properly a quality of riders and applies to the horses figuratively, so the oath concerns horses raiding at dawn. The pilgrimage-camel reading conflicts with the apparent sense of ighārah and, taken with the first five verses, cannot plausibly fit camels travelling from Muzdalifah to Miná. The horses raise naqʿ, clouds of dust, and then penetrate a host: bihi may mean entering the enemy at dawn or entering the dust-covered crowd. Al-Mizan judges the surest reading to concern warriors in God’s way, though God swears by their horses; the repeated fāʾ marks the event sequence.

verses.6: Al-Mizan equates kanūd with kafūr, ungrateful, and describes the human tendency to pursue desire and worldly pleasure until gratitude to the Lord ceases. The verse specifically censures those raided for ingratitude toward Islam, the greatest blessing, which brings a good life here and eternal bliss hereafter. It takes the witness in (100:7) to be al-insān himself: people know their own ingratitude, and witnessing means observing a reality rather than legal testimony. The alternative that the pronoun refers to God does not fit the context.

verses.8: Al-Mizan records readings that intense love of wealth makes people greedy and stingy, or that wealth’s attraction keeps them from God’s due and spending in His way. It tentatively prefers khayr in its unrestricted sense: love of one’s own good and interest is inherent in humanity. The fault begins when worldly display and adornment are mistaken for that good, diverting people from gratitude to their Lord.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains baʿtharah as resurrecting and dispersing what is in graves, and ḥuṣṣila mā fī al-ṣudūr as distinguishing and classifying inward realities such as belief, disbelief, benevolence, and malevolence. It also records that concealed inner secrets may simply be disclosed for recompense alongside outward deeds. The rhetorical question rebukes the ungrateful for ignoring the consequences: with God knows best, the commentary concludes that when bodies are brought from graves and all that souls contain is extracted, their Lord is fully aware and requites them for it all.
